doc.title: "Papa Jack" Laine, Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine and Johnny Wiggs Interview, 1959-02-27

title: Defending Alcide 'Yellow' Nunez as white
summary: Blanche tells how she corrected a writer who thought Yellow Nunez was Black, citing his family, and Laine suggests the nickname caused it.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, now, Parquet, he was sort of a Mexican type, but not Poikins. Not Poikins. I had one fellow, one of these writers come here one day, and he asked me, he said, Yala Nunes, Yala Nunes was a nigger. I said, oh, no.

I said, you mistaken. I said, not Yala Nunes, not Alcide Nunes. I said, no, he wasn't. He was a white man. He's a white man. I knew his sisters, his brothers, his father. We went to his father's wake and funeral. And his sister married Louis Morrow. Morrow that had the grocery net out of Millenburg. Big, fat Louis Morrow. I know who he was married. His sister was married to him. And I knew him. He used to play mandolin. He was a little bit of thing like Georgie Brunis, about 10, 12 years old. He was, mm-mm. How did he get that name, Yellow?
Maybe that's why somebody thought that, because they call him Yellow. He was kind of dark.
He was kind of dark. He was kind of dark, yeah. Yeah.
I know them all. Know his brothers. Know his sisters. Know his father. Know his mother.

I told him. I said, no, sir. He ain't. He said, I want to tell you something. I don't know if you'll get in something. I said, well, no. I said, I want to ask you. He said, ain't this Yala Nunes a nigger too? I said, oh, no. I said, no, sir. He's not. Uh-uh. He's not. He ain't.
Anybody would know I would know.
He said, I, he said, well, I heard that. I said, well, you heard wrong. I said, you heard wrong. Whoever told you that don't know him. They might have him mixed up with somebody else. I said.
I guess they got that from his nickname.

Nickname. Yeah, Yala. Yeah, yeah. Yeah. But now, Paki, you could see, you could tell him. You could tell on him too if you looked at him good. He looked like a Mexican. And there was another one too. He had playing with him, Batiste O'Quin. He was too. Oh, yeah.
So I, I, I let him go because I had two already, you know, lined it up and I didn't want any more.
Yeah. He was too. Because he's people and all. Yeah.
He was. And he was a barber and had a white barber shop. Yeah.
He had a white barber shop. Yeah.
He had a white barber shop. No, but there's a. I knew he was, I knew he had copper in his metal.
